text: ective and non- elective caesarean section, but USA surgical guidelines do not recommend routine prophylaxis in low-risk patients.2 A penicillin or first-generation cephalosporin such as ce- fazolin is often used.2 Early postpartum endometritis has a polymicrobial aetiol- ogy. In one study the most common organisms isolated in- cluded Gardnerella vaginalis, Peptococcus spp., Bacter- oides spp., Staphylococcus epidermidis, group B streptococci, and Ureaplasma urealyticum.3 Chlamydia trachomatis has been implicated more often in late post- partum endometritis, but a wide variety of micro-organ- isms may also be responsible including genital mycoplas- mas and, to a lesser extent, facultative and anaerobic bacteria.4 In the USA, standard empirical therapy for postpartum en- dometritis has been a short course of intravenous antibac- terials, often clindamycin with gentamicin, given until the patient has been afebrile and asymptomatic for 24 to 48 hours and sometimes followed by a course of oral treat- ment, often amoxicillin. A systematic review5 has con- firmed the suitability of clindamycin with gentamicin and indicated that oral therapy is not necessary after successful intravenous therapy.
